title: 2 Chronicles 13:1–12
context: Abijah becomes king of Judah in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year and reigns three years. When he and Jeroboam meet in battle with very large armies, Abijah stands on Mount Zemaraim and addresses Israel. He reminds them that the LORD gave the kingdom to David’s line by a covenant of salt, recounts Jeroboam’s rebellion, and contrasts Israel’s golden calves and self-appointed priests with Judah’s lawful priests, Levites, and daily worship. He ends by warning Israel not to fight against the LORD, the God of their fathers. The parallel in 1 Kings 15:1–8 calls this king Abijam, names his mother as Maacah daughter of Abishalom rather than Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, gives a negative verdict on his reign, and has no record of this speech. These differences are named rather than resolved; the 1 Kings 15 notes discuss them as well.

verses.text: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah begins to reign in Jeroboam’s eighteenth year. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler dates Judah’s king by Israel’s, a reminder that the two kingdoms remain linked despite their division.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the brief notice as introducing a reign the Chronicler presents more favorably than Kings. Shared ground: the parallel in 1 Kings 15:1 calls him Abijam, a difference in name noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah reigns three years; his mother is Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 15:2 names her Maacah daughter of Abishalom, and 2 Chronicles 11:20 calls her “Maacah the granddaughter of Absalom.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note, as the 1 Kings 15 notes do, that many suggest “mother” may mean grandmother or queen mother, but the relationship is not settled. Both traditions name the difference without forcing a resolution.

verses.text: Abijah joined battle with an army of valiant men of war, even four hundred thousand chosen men; and Jeroboam set the battle in array against him with eight hundred thousand chosen men, who were mighty men of valor.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah brings four hundred thousand chosen men against Jeroboam’s eight hundred thousand. Arminian readers note that the numbers are very large and are read in more than one way, and the text gives them as stated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the two-to-one odds as setting up a victory that depends on God. Shared ground: both traditions state the figures as the text gives them, without a speculative harmonization of their size.

verses.text: Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, and said, “Hear me, Jeroboam and all Israel:
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah stands on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and calls on Jeroboam and Israel to listen. Arminian readers note that he appeals to Israel before battle, giving them a chance to reconsider.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the speech as a declaration of God’s purposes for David’s line. Both traditions note that Zemaraim’s exact location is uncertain, though it lies near the border between Judah and Israel.

verses.text: Ought you not to know that the LORD, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt?
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah reminds Israel that the LORD gave the kingdom to David and his sons by a covenant of salt. Arminian readers note the phrase, which elsewhere describes a lasting covenant (Numbers 18:19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant with David as the foundation of Judah’s claim, consistent with how 2 Samuel 7 was treated as shared ground on this site. Shared ground: the speech grounds kingship in God’s promise.

verses.text: Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up, and rebelled against his lord.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah describes Jeroboam as Solomon’s servant who rebelled against his lord. Arminian readers note that this presents Jeroboam’s rise as rebellion, a perspective that differs in emphasis from 1 Kings 11:29–39.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Kings also records the LORD giving ten tribes to Jeroboam through Ahijah, and Abijah’s speech focuses on human rebellion. Both traditions read the speech as Abijah’s argument, not as a full account.

verses.text: Worthless men were gathered to him, wicked fellows who strengthened themselves against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and tender hearted, and could not withstand them.
verses.arminianNotes: Worthless men gathered to Jeroboam against Rehoboam, who was young and could not withstand them. Arminian readers note that Rehoboam was forty-one when he began to reign (12:13), so “young” may mean inexperienced.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Abijah placing blame on Jeroboam’s followers while softening Rehoboam’s failures. Shared ground: both traditions read the description as part of a persuasive speech, with its exact sense read in more than one way.

verses.text: “Now you intend to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David. You are a great multitude, and the golden calves which Jeroboam made you for gods are with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah tells Israel they intend to withstand the LORD’s kingdom in David’s sons, relying on numbers and golden calves. Arminian readers note the contrast between trust in multitudes and idols and trust in God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the phrase “the kingdom of the LORD” as identifying David’s throne with God’s rule. Both traditions read the verse as the heart of Abijah’s charge: Israel’s cause is opposed to God’s own purpose.

verses.text: Haven’t you driven out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves according to the ways of the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes to consecrate himself with a young bull and seven rams may be a priest of those who are no gods.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah accuses Israel of driving out the LORD’s priests and making their own, so that anyone with a bull and seven rams can become a priest. Arminian readers note the echo of 1 Kings 12:31 and 13:33.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the charge as concerning worship done on human terms rather than God’s. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as condemning the corruption of Israel’s priesthood under Jeroboam.

verses.text: “But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests serving the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites in their work.
verses.arminianNotes: Abijah says the LORD is Judah’s God and they have not forsaken Him, with lawful priests and Levites. Arminian readers note the claim of faithfulness, which Kings’ verdict on Abijam (1 Kings 15:3) qualifies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Judah’s lawful worship as the point of contrast, whatever Abijah’s own failings. Both traditions read the claim within the speech and note the different emphases of Kings and Chronicles without resolving them.

verses.text: They burn to the LORD every morning and every evening burnt offerings and sweet incense. They also set the show bread in order on the pure table, and care for the gold lamp stand with its lamps, to burn every evening; for we keep the instruction of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah’s priests offer burnt offerings and incense morning and evening, set the showbread, and tend the lampstand. Arminian readers note the faithful daily worship described, following Exodus 30:7–8 and Leviticus 24:5–9.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the list a picture of worship ordered by God’s instruction. Shared ground: the verse ends with the contrast, “we keep the instruction of the LORD our God, but you have forsaken him,” central to the speech.

verses.text: Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with the trumpets of alarm to sound an alarm against you. Children of Israel, don’t fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers; for you will not prosper.”
verses.arminianNotes: God is at Judah’s head, with priests and trumpets; Abijah warns Israel not to fight against the LORD. Arminian readers see a final appeal for Israel to turn back before it is too late.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trumpets as recalling Numbers 10:9, where God remembers His people in battle. Both traditions read the warning as the climax of the speech, which is kept intact as one unit.
